title: Check a banknote with a counterfeit pen: pin the 1 g note, draw one stroke, then slide it to the mat its mark calls for
instruction: Check the banknote with the counterfeit pen: hold the note flat by one end, draw one stroke at least 1 cm long on it, put the pen back in its cup, then slide the note onto the green mat if the mark is amber or onto the red mat if it is dark, and move your hands away.
context: A familiar moment at a shop counter: a customer pays with a $20, and before it goes in the till the cashier draws a quick line on it with a counterfeit-detector pen. The felt pen's iodine ink reacts with starch in ordinary paper: 'The mark by the pen will be a light amber color on a genuine bill', while on a suspect one 'the mark turns dark brown or black' (QSR Web). A business reports a suspect note to the Secret Service (uscurrency.gov), so here the green mat stands for the till and the red one for a suspect note set aside to report. The physical part is the mark itself: a note weighs about 1 g, so the felt tip's drag slides an unpinned note across the counter and smears the mark. One hand presses the note flat by its end while the other draws one stroke at least 1 cm long and lifts off on the paper; the note is then slid along the counter to its mat.
setup: Two YAM arms at the near edge of a counter; positions are (x forward from the arm bases, y left) in cm. The counter has a light laminate top. A US $20 Federal Reserve note (156 x 66.3 mm, about 1 g) lies flat at (33, 0), its length along y. A counterfeit-detector felt-tip pen (12 mm across, 136 mm long, chisel tip), uncapped, stands tip down in a pen cup (22 mm bore, 45 mm tall) at (24, -20). A green vinyl mat (12 x 20 cm) lies at (33, -27) and a red one at (33, 27). In the standard trial the note is genuine, so the mark comes out amber and the green mat is right; a suspect note (a blank sheet of ordinary starch paper cut to size) marks dark, and the red mat is then right. Each trial uses a fresh note, or a fresh area of it. The arms start at their ready pose.
scoring: Real trial: two cameras (above and level with the counter), a ruler, and the note afterwards. The ink is laid where the felt tip touches the paper while moving across it. A stroke: one touch-down to lift-off; its length is the distance between its mark's two farthest inked points. Pinned: a fingertip pressing the note flat (at or into its face) at one of its ends (the outer 28 mm), not over the stroke. 0.25: the tip touches the note while it is pinned. 0.5: at least one stroke of 10 mm or more, of up to 3, all on the paper with the felt pressed on it (within 0.3 mm of the face for at least half the stroke), pinned throughout, the note moving under 2 mm during it. 0.75: also the pen back in its cup, within 20 degrees of upright, and let go. 1.0: also the note flat on the green mat if the mark is amber, or on the red mat if dark (all four corners over the mat), still, with every fingertip 3 cm or more from the note's plate, held 1 s. 0 at any time: ink on the counter (the tip pressed down off the note), more than 3 strokes, the note lifted more than 5 mm off the counter, the pen dropped, or the note left on the wrong mat. A stroke under which the note slid more than 5 mm is a smear: the score is then at most 0.5.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, 240 Hz. The note is a rigid plate of a US note's size and weight (156 x 66.3 mm, about 1 g, per the BEP), 1 mm thick: it does not bend or crease. Friction is set so that an unpinned note slides under a felt stroke and a pinned one does not. Touch is read from height: the felt within 0.6 mm of the paper, and pressed on it (within 0.3 mm) for half a counted stroke; a fingertip at or into the note's face. The ink is code: dots where the felt moves on the paper.
